Summary
AWS offers a vast array of services that you can use to design and build decoupled and
distributed architectures for your applications. Depending on your business use case, moving
away from a monolithic architecture to a microservices-based, event-driven design provides
several benefits, including reduced single points of failure, independent component scalability,
and improved availability.
To design decoupled architectures, you need a way to separate your application components,
such as frontend and backend services. This is only possible if those components can
communicate in a manner that facilitates independent operation and scalability. The use of
message queuing systems like Amazon SQS plays a critical role in bringing this type of
architecture to life.
Furthermore, designing your application stack so that each component communicates
asynchronously and responds to events as they occur ensures that resources are only
consumed when required. Amazon EventBridge enables you to build such event-driven
applications, helping you avoid idle resources and unnecessary costs.
Finally, when designing complex, distributed, and decoupled architectures, the use of
orchestration services such as Amazon Step Functions gives you the ability to design
application workflows quickly and efficiently.
In the next chapter, you will learn how you can use AWS to analyze the vast array of data your
business collects and stores, both for auditing purposes as well as for specific application
requirements. AWS offers a number of different analytical tools enabling you to perform real-
time data ingestions, perform ad-hoc queries, and even Big Data analytics.

Analytics on AWS
Data is the ultimate currency of the 21st century. Businesses today can either gain a massive
competitive advantage through how they analyze and consume data—or, at worst, go
completely out of business due to data leaks and mismanagement. Companies use data to
understand their markets, identify trends, predict sales, and ultimately gain a competitive
edge.
Furthermore, in idx_83be6256 this era of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI),
understanding idx_31a72635 vast amounts of data has become easier. Organizations can now query their
data, identify complex patterns, and discover outliers much faster. Today's analytical tools,
powered by AI and ML, enable businesses to build solutions that deliver better customer
service, prevent fraud, identify and even predict technical issues or bugs in application code—
and much more.
AWS offers a vast array of analytical services, each designed for different use cases. Whether
you need to process streaming data in real time, run ad-hoc queries, or host an entire data
warehousing solution for your global enterprise, AWS has a service for it.
In this chapter, you will learn about these services, their use cases, and best practices for
configuring them for your specific needs—enabling you to ingest, store, and analyze your data
efficiently.

Streaming data with Amazon Kinesis
A wide range of applications today generate streaming data that must be captured, ingested,
processed, and idx_b1a874f2 analyzed in real time. Examples include logs generated idx_79d40099 by applications (used to
identify access patterns or errors), clickstream data from idx_a0026c0d websites (to uncover trends and
customer behaviors), and Internet of Things (IoT) data (used to monitor sensors, images,
videos, and other connected devices).
Organizations need a reliable mechanism to capture massive volumes of streaming data and
ingest it in real time. This data then needs to be processed and consumed by business
intelligence applications to provide reporting, analytics, and visualizations that support
critical decision-making.

streaming data as it arrives. It enables real-time and near-real-time analytics in a cost-effective
manner—without idx_66a2897a the need to provision or manage any idx_e8625943 underlying infrastructure.
The Amazon Kinesis product suite comprises four key services:

Data Streams and its core capabilities.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

You can create idx_e2e187bb Kinesis data stream applications using the Kinesis Client Library (KCL) and
Amazon idx_c73dcf24 EC2 instances to read data idx_f35217c0 from the streams (known as consumers) and process it
according to your specific business use case. For example, you can use streaming data to build
real-time dashboards, perform anomaly detection to identify fraudulent activities, dynamically
adjust pricing, modify advertising strategies, and much more.
As illustrated in Figure 13.1, Kinesis Data Streams uses the concept of shards, which represent
units of capacity and contain data records within a stream. A stream can consist of multiple
shards, and the total capacity of the stream is the sum of all shard capacities. The overall cost is
determined by the number of shards provisioned, as you are charged per shard per hour.
An important feature of Amazon Kinesis is that data remains in the stream and is accessible for
up to 24 hours by default. This soft limit can be extended to 7 days using the extended data
retention feature. You can also enable long-term data retention, which allows data to be stored
for up to 365 days. This ensures that consuming applications have sufficient time to process all
incoming data streams.
While Amazon Kinesis Data Streams allows you to capture and process streaming data in real
time, it requires you to build and manage the consumer applications that process and store
that data. However, sometimes all you need is a reliable way to deliver large volumes of
streaming idx_2b523556 data directly into storage or analytics services without managing the underlying
infrastructure.
This is where Amazon Data Firehose becomes useful. Amazon Data Firehose automatically
delivers streaming data to a wide range of AWS services and external storage endpoints,
making it easier to load large amounts of data into storage services for later analysis.

Amazon Data Firehose
Businesses need to ingest and load raw data into a wide range of technology services to
perform idx_1c8f9a36 analytics, store historical data for compliance and regulatory requirements, and feed
data into tools like Amazon OpenSearch Service for near real-time analytics using a variety of
business intelligence platforms.
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose can also deliver data to external third-party services such as
Datadog, New Relic, and Splunk, among others, enabling you to continue using the tools your
organization is already familiar with. The service can batch, process, compress, and transform
data before loading it into these third-party targets. You can also encrypt this data to
strengthen your overall security posture.
Kinesis Data Firehose buffers incoming data before delivering it to destinations such as

small delay (typically around 30 to 60 seconds), depending on the buffer size and interval

service.
You can think of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams as a live news broadcast service. You process
data as soon as it's ingested. In contrast, Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is more like a news
highlights feed; you receive updates every minute, bundled and ready for easy consumption.
Amazon Kinesis idx_14a87337 Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose are commonly used to process
streaming data such as application logs, clickstream data, and telemetry information.
However, these services are not designed for continuously streaming video feeds. For video
streaming workloads, AWS provides Amazon Kinesis Video Streams, which you will explore in
the next section.

Businesses today stream a vast array of different content types, and this includes video footage

Amazon Kinesis Video Streams enables you to capture live video data from a wide range of
sources, including CCTV cameras, webcams, drones, and other sources.
Amazon Kinesis Video Streams can also be used to send non-video time-serialized data, such
as audio, radar, thermal imaging, and much more. Amazon Kinesis Video Streams will store
your raw footage in Amazon S3, ensuring high levels of durability for your data. You can then
search for and retrieve those footages based on devices and timestamps.
A key use case for Amazon Kinesis Video Streams is that you can use downstream services on

you can integrate your idx_c8a99295 application architecture to have Amazon Rekognition, a computer

Amazon managed service for Apache Flink
Many businesses idx_cf388918 today use an open-source, real-time idx_ada0eaa7 stream processing engine called Apache
Flink to ingest and process large volumes of data, either in real time or in batches. The service
provides powerful capabilities for running complex computations on streaming data, such as

Rather than idx_2c41a01e designing, building, and managing your own expensive infrastructure to run this

377 Analytics on AWS
Businesses store vast amounts of data in a variety of formats and locations, including
databases and spreadsheets. Often, this data needs to be extracted, transformed into a format
suitable for analysis, and then loaded into services that can perform analytics and support the
creation of business intelligence solutions. The next section introduces you to AWS Glue, a
service idx_fa784ad4 designed specifically for this purpose.
Understanding your data structure with AWS Glue
AWS Glue is a idx_fa819110 serverless Extract, Transform, and Load (ETL) service. Businesses idx_22cad2fa can use
AWS Glue to discover, prepare, enrich, clean, and idx_aec7755a transform data so that downstream services
can easily consume it.

86560.heading: Chapter 13 376
86560.content:
The service offers the ability to crawl your raw datasets and discover their structure, also
known idx_15812598 as a schema. For example, AWS Glue can analyze CSV files to identify column names
and their data types (such as string, number, or Boolean). This makes it easier to ingest the
idx_1726d081 data into analytics and business intelligence (BI) tools for further analysis and visualization.
You can use the crawler to scan various data repositories, classify datasets, and infer their
schemas. The resulting metadata is then stored in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which can be
used to automatically generate ETL scripts that transform, flatten, or enrich your datasets. You
can also define events or schedules to run crawlers regularly against your ingested datasets as
batch jobs, ensuring your data remains continuously prepared for analysis by downstream
services such as Amazon QuickSight and Amazon Athena.
While idx_6617261b some customers continuously stream, process, and analyze idx_3d44fd22 data in real time, others may
only need a cost-effective approach to run ad-hoc queries against data that has been captured
over time. In such cases, hosting a fully-fledged database or data warehouse solution like
Amazon Redshift can be excessive. The next section introduces you to Amazon Athena, a
service designed to run ad-hoc queries directly against data stored in Amazon S3, without the
need to provision or manage traditional database infrastructure.
Performing ad hoc analytics with Amazon Athena
Many companies store data as files in object storage services such as Amazon S3. Much of this
data idx_d2effedb is only occasionally accessed idx_68c297a0 for point-in-time analysis and then stored for historical
reference. In other words, these datasets do not need to be stored in active idx_bb3d3bbd databases such idx_2617ec9a as
Amazon RDS or NoSQL databases like Amazon DynamoDB, since the data is not regularly
queried.
Nevertheless, ad-hoc analysis of such data, for example, running daily batch jobs or
performing historical analysis, may still be required. In such cases, provisioning entire

86561.content:
Chapter 13 378
databases and ingesting large datasets for a one-time or infrequent analysis can be
unnecessary and costly.
AWS offers Amazon Athena, a fully idx_0cc5e87e managed, serverless query service that allows you to
interactively analyze raw data directly in Amazon S3 using standard SQL (Structured Query
Language). You idx_a63835bd don't need to provision or manage any infrastructure, nor do you need to spin
up expensive database instances to perform ad-hoc queries.
Amazon idx_3b1f889f Athena uses Presto, an open-source SQL query engine designed for running fast,
interactive queries. It supports ANSI SQL, enabling you to work with features like large joins,
window functions, and arrays.
With idx_3b471113 Amazon Athena, you can run queries idx_4c0c2aa8 against structured and semi-structured datasets. To
perform your queries, you must create a database table within Athena that defines the schema
of your raw data stored in Amazon S3. This means Athena only needs to understand the data
structure; the data itself remains in S3. Athena simply uses the table definition to query the
underlying raw data, without needing to move or ingest it.
You can also use AWS Glue, which you learned about in the previous section, to crawl your raw
data in Amazon S3 and automatically generate the required schema for your Athena tables.
Once your tables are registered, you can run SQL SELECT statements to query them, and you
can even store query results in Amazon S3 in a location of your choice. A typical use case where
Belly Brew Co. Limited might use Amazon Athena is if it needs to run a query like "What were
our top 10 Kombucha flavors last month?"
In the next idx_d27c15f7 section, you will learn about Amazon OpenSearch Service and Amazon EMR,
which idx_339c0971 offer additional capabilities for large-scale search and big data analytics.
Searching and processing large-scale data with
Amazon OpenSearch Service and Amazon EMR
While idx_c501095c Amazon Athena is designed to analyze idx_9656e2ef static and historical idx_4be7d515 data directly from idx_415b6cec Amazon
S3, there are times when you idx_af3b75c2 need a robust, ultra-fast search solution capable idx_589d2b69 of delivering
results within milliseconds. That's where Amazon OpenSearch Service comes in.
For example, you might use Athena to run a query like, "What were our top 10 Kombucha
flavors last month?" Whereas with OpenSearch, you could perform a search like "Show me all
error logs idx_2959efea containing the word 'timeout' from the last hour."
Amazon OpenSearch Service is designed for searching, filtering, and visualizing log or text
data in real time. It scales seamlessly, supporting up to 25 petabytes of attached storage and up
to 1002 data nodes running on Amazon EC2 instances.

OpenSearch enables you to perform full-text search, log analytics, and clickstream analytics.

Additionally, Amazon OpenSearch Service includes a vector engine that provides vector
storage and search capabilities for ML-augmented applications and generative AI solutions—

Another service idx_5cf62505 offered by AWS is Amazon EMR (Elastic MapReduce). This service enables

Amazon Rekognition can detect objects and text in images and video, as well as compare faces,
perform facial analysis, and identify attributes, such as age, gender, and emotions.

Another capability of Amazon Rekognition idx_8b1514bf is Face Liveness. Many applications require live

KYC (Know Your Customer) verification. In addition to uploading identity documents, you
are often required to log in to a web app using your mobile device and camera, where the app

Converting text to speech with Amazon Polly
Amazon Polly is an idx_f37b0a7c artificial intelligence service that uses deep learning to synthesize speech
into a human-like voice with just text inputs. You can select from a wide range of voices across
different accents and languages for both genders.
You can send your text data to Amazon Polly via API calls and have it immediately converted to
an audio stream, which you can play back as part of your application. Amazon Polly supports
standard audio formats like MP3.
Amazon Polly also idx_1c9a9725 offers Neural Text-to-Speech (NTTS) voices that support features like
Newscaster idx_18422dc8 speaking styles, enabling the delivery of flash news updates by TV and radio
newscaster organizations.
With Amazon Polly, you can also use custom lexicons to modify pronunciation for particular
words, use acronyms, and neologisms. To customize pronunciations, you can upload an XML
file with lexical entries. For example, some TTS systems pronounce the common English word
"often" incorrectly as "off-ten." Any time Polly encounters that word in your speech output, it
will use your custom pronunciation.
An example lexicon XML file is provided as follows:
<lexicon version="1.0"
xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/01/pronunciation-lexicon"
alphabet="ipa"
xml:lang="en-US">
<lexeme>
<grapheme>often</grapheme>
<!-- Correct pronunciation: "aw-fn" -->
<phoneme>ˈɔːfən</phoneme>
</lexeme>
</lexicon>
Notice how you can use the <phoneme> element to explicitly define the correct pronunciation.
This allows Amazon Polly to speak words exactly the way you intend, ensuring natural-
sounding and accurate text-to-speech output—even for words that are commonly
mispronounced.
You can use Amazon Polly idx_0caa704f for a wide range of voice applications, such as interactive voice
response (IVR) systems, educational idx_49a8a007 content narration, accessibility tools, real-time

announcements, audiobook generation, and creating natural-sounding voices for websites and
mobile apps.
After looking at how Amazon Polly turns text into speech, it is useful to look at services that
work in the other direction or with related language-processing tasks, such as converting
speech to text, translating content, and extracting text from documents.

and text extraction
AWS provides several AI services that help you process spoken, written, and document-based
content. Amazon Transcribe converts speech into text, Amazon Translate converts text
between languages, and Amazon Textract extracts text and structured data from documents
and images.
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Transcribe is a idx_cf42a789 fully managed automatic speech-to-text transcription service. You

Amazon Transcribe can help you extract business insights from meetings, customer calls, and
video files. You can also use it to automatically transcribe clinical conversations, and the
service is fully HIPAA compliant. For added privacy, you can have sensitive and personally

decide on auto scaling policies, and define how your load balancers should be configured.

Next, you will learn more about some of the core components of AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
Core components of AWS Elastic Beanstalk
When working with idx_065ace85 AWS Elastic Beanstalk, you idx_4a6e03c5 create an application. Think of this as a folder
in Elastic Beanstalk that groups related environments and versions of the same app. It is within
the application container that you manage all the Elastic Beanstalk objects related to your
application.
An application can have multiple versions, enabling you to test the differences between them.
It is a pointer to a ZIP/WAR file in an Amazon S3 bucket that contains the application code.
Before you deploy your application, you idx_6f1abcd4 must create an environment, which is a collection of
AWS resources that will run the application, such as EC2 instances, load balancers, runtimes,
and language frameworks. Each environment can only run one application version at a time;
however, you can run multiple environments simultaneously. This is how you can host
different stages of your application, such as:
Development: used by developers to build new features or fix bugs
Testing: used for alpha and beta testing
Production: the live environment accessed by end users
When you create an environment, you must idx_934bdbee define the environment tier. The environment
tier describes how traffic reaches your application and tells AWS what resources to provision.
There are two tiers:
Web Server environment: used for idx_a96b209c applications' HTTP and HTTPS requests (for
example, websites and API calls)
Worker environment: used for idx_c348b00c background processing applications that receive jobs
from a queue
Figure 15.1 depicts the two Elastic Beanstalk environment tiers for a typical application that
comprises a frontend and backend workload.

The application is served by an Application Load Balancer that accepts requests using

The Web Server Tier comprises the EC2 instances, which host the frontend user

The Worker Tier is designed to process background application logic. It is supported by

SQS queue, which is designed to decouple the application stack. The Elastic Beanstalk
service will install a daemon on each EC2 instance in the fleet. The daemon is used to
read messages from the SQS queue and send this data to the application servers
running in the worker environment for processing.
The Amazon SQS queue is used to store messages as requests from the front-end web
server tier, which the resources in the worker tier will pull based on capacity and

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is a idx_43936472 process by which you define and describe your infrastructure
resources and their configurations in a scripted template written using a data serialization
language such as YAML or JSON.
Data-serialization languages are used to convert structured data into a format that can be
stored, transmitted, and read by another system, without losing its meaning.
AWS CloudFormation uses idx_70392fc4 data-serialization languages like YAML and JSON to read the
structured description of your AWS resources, build a dependency graph, and then provision
the infrastructure automatically. This is also known as declarative scripting.
This is different from imperative scripting using languages like Python or Java, which require
you to explicitly describe the step-by-step instructions on how to carry out those
configurations.

describes the resources to provision, along with mandatory and optional configuration options
required to provision the resources.
For example, if you need to deploy an EC2 instance in the default VPC, in a default subnet, and
attach it to the default security group, you can provide a CloudFormation template such as the

so you must provide an AMI ID that exists in the region where the resources are being

Some properties such as InstanceType, SubnetId, and SecurityGroupIds may need to

In the next section, you will learn more about CloudFormation stacks.
CloudFormation stacks
When you create and upload a idx_62bddac1 CloudFormation template, you deploy what is known as a
Stack. A stack idx_60d7a078 is a collection of one or more AWS resources that are deployed and managed as a
single unit using CloudFormation. For example, using a single template, you can provision a
VPC, load balancers, auto-scaling groups to provision EC2 instances, and even a backend
Amazon RDS database, all part of that single stack.
How you build out your stack deployment is also critical. For example, you can use more
advanced techniques to modularize the various infrastructure elements of your environment
as separate templates. You can then use either:
Cross-Stack References: Where you build a base stack, such as a VPC, and allow other
stacks to reference idx_b362ab93 values from it (for example, Subnet IDs or Security Groups) so that
compute or database resources can be deployed into the same underlying environment
without being part of the same stack.
Nested Stacks: Where you modularize each infrastructure element, such as VPCs, EC2
instances, and RDS instances, as separate templates and invoke them from a main
parent template idx_52f4ac16 to build a complete end-to-end infrastructure for an application. This
allows you to organize infrastructure into logical components while still managing
everything through a single parent stack, making updates and ongoing management
easier

stack. AWS will then terminate all the resources it created following your template. This

AWS CloudFormation change sets
If you need to change the idx_0a59ce4c configuration of your cloud resources to cope with changing
requirements or demand, you need a way to upgrade or modify existing resources without
having to rebuild the entire stack. This is particularly true if the change you need to make
should not affect the application.
AWS CloudFormation offers a idx_167af945 feature known as Change Sets, which is where you upload a
modified version of your template or even supply a new template as a change to the existing
stack configuration. AWS CloudFormation will then provide a visual representation of your
proposed changes and notify you if the change will require resource replacements.

Change sets are particularly useful in highlighting how the change proposed will impact the
existing architecture and if any resources will be affected. You can then take any necessary
precautions, such as performing backups and taking manual snapshots before executing the
change.
AWS CloudFormation makes it easy to build infrastructure solutions in a consistent, repeatable
manner with predictable outcomes. You can build a wide range of templates to quickly deploy

your resources using idx_ef590fcf CloudFormation rather than manually configuring each resource using

In addition to automating your infrastructure provisioning and deployment using tools like
Elastic Beanstalk and CloudFormation, you must also consider your application lifecycle that
runs on the provisioned infrastructure. Modern architectures recommend applying DevOps
principles and best practices when designing how your applications are deployed, updated,
and released into production environments. The next section introduces you to this concept
and the tools offered by AWS to build an effective DevOps pipeline.
Introducing CI/CD with AWS developer tools
Managing the application lifecycle is crucial to ensure that users always have access to the
latest and most reliable version of an application, without bugs or performance issues. This
means development teams must continuously enhance the application, introduce new
features based on customer feedback, and resolve issues in a timely manner. In addition,
releasing the application into production must follow a carefully planned strategy, ensuring
that new features and bug fixes are deployed with minimal disruption and that rollbacks are
simple if something goes wrong.
DevOps idx_f3fe68ae is a set of practices that brings development (Dev) and operations (Ops) teams
together to collaborate across the entire application lifecycle. Rather than delivering large
releases every few months or once a year, DevOps promotes small, frequent, and incremental
releases aligned with the principles of CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous
Delivery/Deployment). Instead of working in silos, DevOps encourages automation and
continuous feedback, allowing applications to be released faster, more reliably, and with fewer
errors.
AWS provides a wide range of tools and services to build, test, deploy, and operate
applications, while improving quality, stability, and customer satisfaction.
In the following subsections, we will look at a high-level overview of some of these tools.
AWS CodeCommit
Developers write and maintain code for their applications, which must be continuously
updated, revised, and versioned as new features are added and bugs are fixed. AWS
CodeCommit is a idx_991b448f fully managed, secure source control service that hosts Git-based
repositories, enabling teams to manage source code versions and track changes efficiently.
CodeCommit can be used to store application source code, configuration files, scripts, and
documentation. It works with standard Git tools and commands, making it easy for developers
439 Automation, Deployment, and Additional AWS Services
who already use Git on other platforms to adopt CodeCommit without changing their existing

workflows.
AWS CodeBuild
AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed idx_fb5388ba build service. Developers use CodeBuild to compile source
code, run unit tests, and build artifacts that can then be deployed on AWS. There is no need to
provision your own build servers, and the service offers prepackaged build environments for
popular languages and build tools. All you need to do is provide a buildspec file, which is a
collection of build commands and related settings, in YAML format. AWS CodeBuild uses this
file to run a build.
Finally, you are charged on a pay-as-you-go model, making the offering very cost-effective
rather than hosting your own build servers.
AWS CodeDeploy
Once an application has been idx_1d0ab8c4 built and compiled, AWS CodeDeploy can be used to automate
the deployment of the application to Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic Container
Service (ECS), AWS idx_f717dda0 Lambda functions, and on-premises servers. CodeDeploy helps ensure
that application updates are delivered in a consistent and repeatable way.
CodeDeploy deploys application revisions and supporting artifacts that are typically stored in
services such as Amazon S3 or external repositories like GitHub and BitBucket. The service
enables rapid and reliable application releases, including updating Lambda function versions,
while helping to avoid application downtime during deployments. This is achieved using
different deployment strategies, such as in-place deployments, where instances are updated
gradually (for example, by taking a defined number of instances offline at a time), and blue/
green deployments, where the existing application version (blue environment) continues to
run while a new version is deployed to a separate environment (green environment). Once
testing and approvals are complete, traffic can be shifted to the new version.
One of the key benefits of idx_91fbf227 AWS CodeDeploy is its centralized control over application
deployments, including the ability to monitor deployment status, stop deployments, and roll
back automatically if errors occur.
AWS CodePipeline
AWS CodePipeline is a fully managed idx_860db6f5 continuous delivery solution you can use to automate
your application releases and updates. CodePipeline integrates with the previously mentioned
tools (CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy) to automate the build, test, and deployment
of your application releases every time your code changes, as depicted in the following
workflow in Figure 15.3:

The following steps explain the workflow of the AWS CodePipeline service:
The developer pushes the source code to the AWS CodeCommit repository
A commit to CodeCommit triggers an AWS CodePipeline workflow
The Source stage of CodePipeline pulls the latest code from the CodeCommit repository
The Build stage uses AWS CodeBuild to compile, test, and package the application
The Deploy stage uses AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the application
AWS idx_93e921d8 CodeDeploy then deploys the application to the target EC2 instance
CodePipeline doesn't store code, build applications, or deploy workloads; it simply
orchestrates the entire CI/CD workflow.
In the next section, you will learn how developers can use AI tools on AWS to help them write
code and design application workflows using a product called Amazon Q.
Introducing Amazon Q
Amazon Q is a idx_f298acd5 fully managed generative AI service that acts as an intelligent assistant for
working with AWS. Using natural language processing (NLP), you can ask questions about

Summary
In this chapter, you discovered how businesses want to be able to focus on their application
design and development rather than the underlying heavy lifting associated with
infrastructure provisioning, deployment, and management. Companies do not want to spend
hours maintaining and managing their infrastructure and instead need to focus on building
new features and resolving bugs within their applications.
Furthermore, the ability to automate infrastructure provisioning and management in a
repeatable and consistent manner is critical to avoid potential discrepancies in minute
configuration items of those resources, which often lead to confusion and delayed
troubleshooting exercises.
To help customers automate and manage their infrastructure resources efficiently, AWS offers
PaaS tools such as Elastic Beanstalk and IaC solutions such as CloudFormation.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk is designed to help developers focus on their code. Developers can
upload their code in a supported language and framework and have Elastic Beanstalk
provision all the necessary infrastructure resources to host the application.
AWS CloudFormation is an IaC platform, enabling you to define your infrastructure resources
using YAML or JSON templates. You can create templates that define complete end-to-end
architecture patterns and deploy the required resources as stacks fully managed by the
CloudFormation service.
Finally, you learned about various developer tools that support your application and software
development lifecycle (SDLC) process using CI/CD services such as AWS CodeCommit,
CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline.
In the next chapter, you will learn about monitoring and managing your resources on AWS.
While architecting, building, and deploying solutions play an important role as a Cloud
Practitioner, supporting existing environments, managing, and maintaining workloads so that
they operate at optimal levels is just as critical. The chapter introduces you to tools that help
you analyze the health and performance of your resources and take appropriate actions to
ensure reliability and stability. You will also learn how to audit access and enforce governance
while also understanding concepts related to change management. In addition, you will learn
about various tools to help you efficiently manage fleets of resources.

Management and Governance on

As a cloud practitioner, you must ensure that the wide range of resources you provision to host
your application are highly available, secure, and perform as expected. You must continuously
monitor your underlying resources and identify any potential performance issues that could
cause bottlenecks. These issues should be addressed at the earliest and, with the help of
monitoring and logging solutions available on AWS, even prevented.
You must also be able to audit your environment to ensure that you prevent any unauthorized
access or deployments and detect anomalies that may indicate performance or security issues.
Furthermore, you must enforce proper change management processes to ensure that all
changes made to resources are compliant with organizational requirements and to prevent
unauthorized changes.
Finally, as part of your day-to-day management, you must also be able to effectively manage
your resources—such as patching, performing updates, and automating maintenance tasks.
In this chapter, you will look at a series of AWS services that enable you to effectively monitor
and manage your AWS resources. You can use these services to ensure your resources operate
efficiently and within acceptable performance standards. You can also audit and log all
requests made in your AWS account to ensure you have a trail of all activities, enabling you to
stay compliant. Finally, you can enforce rules to ensure resources provisioned, or changes made
to existing ones, are in accordance with business goals and objectives.
The following topics are covered in this chapter:
Observing workloads with Amazon CloudWatch
Meeting compliance requirements with AWS CloudTrail
Managing change control with AWS Config
Automating resource administration with AWS Systems Manager
Improving workloads with AWS Trusted Advisor
Observing workloads with Amazon CloudWatch
Amazon CloudWatch is a fully idx_2c9b9c0d managed monitoring and logging service designed to help you
monitor and analyze the health of your AWS resources and applications. With Amazon
CloudWatch, you can see how your resources are performing in real time. You can collect
measurements (called metrics) from your idx_b40742cd resources hosted on AWS as well as from on-
premises locations.
A metric represents a time-ordered set of data points that are published to CloudWatch. An
example of a metric is CPU Utilization for an EC2 instance, expressed as a percentage over time.
If a particular instance is consuming more than 95% CPU utilization for an extended period,
you may wish to investigate it, as this could affect performance for your end users.
You can also use Amazon CloudWatch to collect application log data as key-value pairs, which
can be used to identify issues with applications such as errors, timeouts, and more. Thus, in

addition to capturing metric data from resources such as EC2 instances, RDS databases, and
DynamoDB tables, you can also obtain logging information for applications, such as Apache
web servers, Nginx, WordPress, and more.
Some typical use cases for Amazon CloudWatch include the following:
Infrastructure monitoring and troubleshooting: Monitor resource metrics and logs
and visualize trends over time to identify potential bottlenecks. This can be used to
conduct root cause analysis to resolve incidents and problems.
Proactive resource optimization: Configure alarms that monitor metric values and
are triggered when defined thresholds are crossed for a specified period. You can also
define automated remediation actions, such as configuring Auto Scaling to launch
additional resources to distribute load or restarting or terminating instances.

Amazon CloudWatch offers a wide range of built-in metrics across its vast array of services and
resources. However, you may also need to collect custom metrics, as discussed next:
Built-in metrics: Amazon CloudWatch allows you to collect a wide range of default
metrics. These metrics are captured from the underlying infrastructure, such as the
host machines and the hypervisor layer. An example of this is CPU utilization, which
captures how much CPU is being consumed from the allocated capacity at the
hypervisor level. Other examples include disk read/write and data transfer metrics.
Custom metrics: If you need to capture operating system-level or application-level
metrics, you must install a CloudWatch agent on the resource, such as an EC2 instance.
Examples include web application load times, request error rates, and more. Another
example of a custom metric is operating system memory consumption. This is because,
unlike CPU utilization, which monitors underlying hardware CPU usage patterns,
memory metrics operate at the OS level and are not monitored by default.
While capturing all these idx_a1f0e6ea different metrics over a period is useful, the ability to present the
data in an easily digestible form is crucial for quickly identifying trends and issues. Amazon
CloudWatch offers the ability to create custom dashboards, which are discussed next.
CloudWatch dashboards
Amazon CloudWatch idx_7f13bb40 offers a dashboard feature enabling you to present captured metrics and
logging data that offer visualization capabilities through charts and graphs.
You can use CloudWatch dashboards to provide insights into your resources' health across
AWS accounts and regions using the cross-account functionality and integrate this with AWS
organizations. This enables you to create cross-account dashboards.

In addition to monitoring your resources using CloudWatch dashboards, you can also create
alarms that trigger when idx_40ea7fe9 specified threshold values are breached. This is discussed in the next
section.
CloudWatch alarms
You can idx_89f7fca5 configure CloudWatch alarms to monitor idx_46df14fd a given resource's metrics, for example, the
average CPU utilization of an EC2 instance. If the metric crosses a specific threshold value that
you define, it can trigger an alarm. Note that the alarm will only trigger once the threshold
value is breached for more than a defined period. This helps prevent false positives caused by
momentary spikes.
For example, you may wish to trigger an alarm if the CPU utilization on an EC2 instance is over
90% for more than 15 minutes.

86687.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
86687.heading: Chapter 16 454

CloudWatch alarms can be in any one of three states:
OK: Occurs when the idx_c830b23f metric is within the range defined as acceptable
Alarm: Occurs when the metric is outside the specified range. This can be either above
or below the defined threshold
Insufficient data: Occurs when the data needed to determine the alarm state is
missing or idx_a52ec6a4 incomplete. Typically, an alarm is in this state when it is first created, while
it begins collecting metric data
Once an alarm has been triggered, you can automate certain actions to be taken in response.
These include:
Simple Notification Service (SNS) notification: You can send an automatic
notification to idx_f28f8993 an administrator or push the notification to an application or a Lambda
function to perform an automated remediation task
Auto Scaling action: For EC2 instances, you can trigger an Auto Scaling action when
the alarm is triggered to launch or terminate instances as required, ensuring that the
metric falls back within acceptable ranges
EC2 action: You can configure an alarm to trigger an EC2 instance action, such as
stopping or restarting the instance. For certain instance types, you can also perform an
instance recovery, which means the instance is relaunched on different host hardware.
This is particularly useful if the underlying hardware on which the EC2 instance was
originally running is experiencing an issue
You can also publish your idx_2159241a alarms to CloudWatch dashboards, giving you instant visibility
when alarms are triggered.

In addition to metrics, CloudWatch allows you to ingest logging data across both AWS services

CloudWatch logs
Amazon CloudWatch idx_ac867e28 also offers the ability to capture logging data across a wide range of AWS
services, as well as third-party applications that you host on Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon
ECS clusters, and AWS Lambda functions. For example, you can ingest VPC Flow Logs into
CloudWatch Logs, which allows you to analyze network traffic flowing into and out of your
VPCs. You can also capture logs from services such as AWS CloudTrail, Amazon Route 53, and
many more. Examples of third-party application logs that you can capture include web server
access logs, error logs, and operating system event logs.
You can ingest logs regardless of their source, and they are stored as a series of time-ordered
events that you can query, analyze, search, and filter for specific patterns or error codes. You
can also visually analyze your logging data using CloudWatch dashboards.
Logging data can be retained indefinitely for historical analysis, although many organizations
configure retention periods ranging from 1 day to 10 years to meet compliance requirements.
You can also archive your logging data to Amazon S3 buckets and use one of the Amazon S3
Glacier storage classes to keep costs to a minimum.
In the next section, you will learn idx_94309819 about another management and governance service known
as AWS CloudTrail. This service is designed to help you audit access patterns and enforce
governance and compliance.
Meeting compliance requirements with AWS
CloudTrail
As part of your overall idx_0fc50997 management, governance, and security toolkit, you must monitor access
patterns and track all actions that take place in your AWS account – be they provisioning or
terminating resources, or even as simple as an IAM user logging into your AWS account, having
read access to those resources and applications. Amazon CloudTrail is an auditing service that
records every single API call made to your AWS account and the resources contained within.
Amazon CloudTrail is enabled by default and records all activities you perform in your AWS
account. For example, if a user Alice logs in to the account and launches an EC2 instance, and
then later terminates it, all these individual actions are recorded as depicted in the following
screenshot in Figure 16.5.
457 Management and Governance on AWS
Figure 16.5: Amazon CloudTrail event history
With Amazon CloudTrail, you can monitor and enforce compliance and governance by
responding to the idx_a11767cc recorded time-ordered series of events that take place in your AWS
account. You can ingest these events into Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon EventBridge to

86689.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
86689.heading: Chapter 16 456
86689.content:
trigger automated remediation actions, such as invoking AWS Lambda functions or sending
alert notifications using Amazon SNS.
Amazon CloudTrail provides a history of both API and non-API activities. API activities
include actions such as launching an EC2 instance or deleting an Amazon S3 bucket. Non-API
activities include actions such as logging in to the AWS Management Console.
Amazon CloudTrail allows you to record the following types of events:
Management events: These provide idx_db0a2cb3 information about management operations that
you perform in your AWS account. Also known as control plane operations, examples
include API calls such as the RunInstances operation when you launch a new EC2
instance. Management events include both write-only and read-only events.
For example, when Alice launches an EC2 instance (as shown in Figure 16.5), she
performs a write-only event. A read-only event would include an API operation such as
DescribeInstances, which returns a list of EC2 instances without making any
changes. Management events can also include non-API activities, such as when a user
logs in to the AWS Management Console.
Data events: These provide information about operations performed on or within a
resource in your AWS account. For example, when you upload an object to an Amazon
S3 bucket, you perform the PutObject API operation. Another example of a data event
is adding items to a DynamoDB table, which results in a PutItem API operation.
•
•

86690.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
86690.heading: Chapter 16 458
86690.content:
Chapter 16 458
Data events are idx_dd5d52ef known as data plane operations and are generally high volume. Data
events are not logged by default, and you must explicitly configure a trail and specify
the supported resources or resource types for which you want to collect these events.
Insight events: These provide details about unusual activities in your AWS account.
You must idx_2efea8ca enable Insight events to allow CloudTrail to detect such behavior. For
example, if your account normally logs one or two Amazon S3 DeleteBucket API calls
per minute, but suddenly starts logging 200 DeleteBucket calls per minute, this may
be recorded as unusual activity.
Amazon CloudTrail Events idx_ab334d38 stores all management events for up to 90 days, which you can view
in the console or download. Furthermore, the event history will not provide any information
on data events—for these, you must create a trail, which is discussed in the next section.
Regional and global trails
If you need to store data idx_3a5f40dc events or management events beyond the default 90-day retention
period, you must create a specific Amazon CloudTrail trail. A trail is a configuration that
enables CloudTrail to record specific types of events and store them in Amazon S3 and
optionally in AWS CloudWatch Logs.
Trails can be configured to record events from a single region or across all regions:
All-Regions trail: CloudTrail records events in each AWS region and delivers them as
log files to the Amazon S3 bucket that you specify. When you configure CloudTrail to
record events from all regions, any new regions launched by AWS are automatically
included. The All-Regions trail is also the default option when you create a trail using
the CloudTrail console.
Single-Region trail: In some cases, you may only require trail data from a specific
region. You can configure a trail to record log files and event data from a single region
and have them delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket of your choice.
You can also idx_bc09fde2 create an AWS Organization trail, which records events from the management
account as well as all member accounts in the AWS Organizations environment. This approach
ensures that you record important management events across all member accounts,
supporting centralized auditing, and compliance requirements.
In the next section, you will learn about another service that allows you to analyze and
evaluate changes to your idx_629324d4 resources over a period. This is particularly useful when you want to
enforce change management processes and ensure that any configuration you implement is in
alignment with corporate governance and rules.
•
•

459 Management and Governance on AWS
Managing change control with AWS Config
AWS Config is a service idx_3a1e37d1 that enables you to monitor how your resources are configured and

86691.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
86691.heading: Chapter 16 458
86691.content:
track changes to those configurations over time. You can also gain insights into how those
resources were configured in the past, including resources that have since been deleted.
In addition, you can define rules to ensure that any resources created are compliant with
predefined configurations. For example, you may wish to enforce a rule that all Amazon S3
buckets have versioning enabled. If versioning has not been set, AWS Config will flag the
bucket as non-compliant.
With AWS Config, you can monitor changes to individual configuration items of your
resources. A configuration item is a point-in-time snapshot of the attributes for a given
resource in your AWS account. A configuration item includes information such as metadata,

Improving workloads with AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Trusted Advisor is a service idx_dd562b5a that enables you to analyze your workloads and how they
are configured against AWS-recommended best practices across five different categories.
These best practices help you identify opportunities to improve resource performance,
reliability, security, and cost-effectiveness. AWS Trusted Advisor uses a color-coded system to
highlight key configuration findings, as follows:
Green: Trusted Advisor has not identified any issues, and your resources comply with
best practices
Yellow: Trusted Advisor detects a potential issue and recommends reviewing your
configuration. For example, if you are consuming more than 80% of a particular service
limit, this will be highlighted
Red: Trusted Advisor recommends that you take immediate action to resolve critical
issues. For example, if you have opened port 3389 (RDP) to allow access to a Windows
EC2 instance from the entire internet (0.0.0.0/0), this is considered a security risk
The five categories used idx_0bc50812 to guide how your resources should be configured are:
Performance: Provides recommendations on how you can modify your existing
infrastructure architecture and configurations to improve performance. This category
helps identify over-utilized resources and recommends upgrades where appropriate
Security: Reports on resources that are not configured in accordance with security best
practices. For example, if multi-factor authentication (MFA) is not enabled on the
root user idx_5b28085f account, AWS highlights this as a critical security risk.
Fault tolerance: Identifies resources that should be reconfigured to improve resilience
and reduce single points of failure
Cost optimization: Performs checks to identify opportunities to reduce costs and
avoid waste. This may include recommendations such as moving from On-Demand
pricing to Reserved Instances or using appropriate Savings Plans
Service limits: Checks whether your AWS resources are approaching service limits or
quotas and alerts you accordingly
AWS Trusted Advisor is a go-to tool for obtaining a detailed breakdown of how your AWS
resources are configured and for analyzing recommendations to align them with industry best
practices and AWS guidance.

Security Fundamentals and Tools

Over the last few years, you may have heard about several high-profile security breaches and
data leaks involving household brand names in the news. Cyber-attacks of all kinds have been
on the rise, and given the advancement in technology, you would be forgiven for thinking that
such security issues would decrease.
On the contrary, popular online applications offering email services, trading platforms, and
storage services have had to enforce stricter security protocols to protect user accounts. These
include idx_c35debec mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA) and idx_f15fdf31 stricter Know Your Customer
(KYC) documentation requirements. These measures have become necessary in recent years.
In this chapter, you will learn about the importance of designing, deploying, and managing
your applications and idx_c6e03894 resources using a zero-trust approach. You will explore the
fundamentals of the Shared Responsibility Model between the cloud provider and the
customer, understand the need for regulatory compliance, and discover the various AWS tools
and services that can help you efficiently secure your workloads.
As you architect and build solutions, you must integrate security measures and protocols in
accordance with best practices at every layer — from the physical infrastructure where
resources reside, such as cloud provider data centers, through the network and transport
layers, all the way up to the application layer. Each layer must be protected.
The following topics are covered in this chapter:

Applying the Shared Responsibility Model
With on-premises idx_28777c6b networks and data centers, you are solely responsible for the security you
architect and implement for your applications — from the physical security that determines
who can enter data center facilities and server rooms, through to how the application is made
accessible over the Internet and other external networks.
With cloud providers, however, the responsibility for designing and implementing the same

between the customer and the cloud service provider.
You can rest assured that AWS designs and enforces physical security measures to ensure that
only authorized personnel are granted access to the underlying infrastructure hosting your
cloud resources and applications. AWS implements security controls to protect the physical
network, underlying firewall services, and all security layers up to the hypervisor that runs
your compute resources.
With managed services such as Amazon RDS and DynamoDB, additional security protocols are

Meeting compliance requirements with AWS

AWS offers compliance idx_7bb1165a programs aligned with a idx_32278b54 wide range of global regulatory and legal
standards. Depending on the nature of your business, you may need to ensure that any
applications or workloads hosted on AWS meet specific compliance requirements. To that end,
you can verify whether AWS participates in the necessary compliance programs.
For example, if you plan to process and store credit card information, your application must
meet the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS). At the same time, AWS
must ensure idx_3ad67a7e that the underlying infrastructure used to host the application is also aligned with
these requirements.
Similarly, if you are a healthcare organization based in the United States, you must comply
with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996. This means
your application idx_3fed22df must be designed to be HIPAA-compliant. Any patient information stored
must be secured, confidential, and encrypted. Access idx_92cab3ab to patient Protected Health Information
(PHI) must be granted only to authorized personnel.
While there is no formal HIPAA idx_d8e12935 certification for a cloud service provider (CSP) such as AWS,
AWS aligns with HIPAA's risk management expectations through frameworks such as
FedRAMP and NIST 800-53. These are higher security standards that map to the HIPAA
Security Rule and support compliance.
In addition to its wide range of compliance idx_692d92f3 programs, AWS also offers AWS Artifact — a self-
service portal that provides on-demand access to security and compliance reports (such as ISO,
SOC, and PCI) as well as idx_05f711c3 agreements idx_d4751e38 like the Business Associate Addendum (BAA) and Non-

In Chapter 6, you were introduced to Amazon S3 encryption, which focused on how you can
encrypt the data you store in your Amazon S3 buckets. However, encryption options can also
be applied to other idx_c18e5563 resource idx_90ef7dd9 types, such as encrypting your EBS volumes or RDS Databases. In
the next section, you will learn more about encryption options on AWS.
Securing data with AWS encryption services
Encryption is the process of making data unreadable to unauthorized users and applications.
Plain text data is scrambled using an encryption key and an algorithm. The only way to get
back the plain text is to have the appropriate decryption key.
There are two types of encryption:
Encryption in transit: This is idx_d2d0096e when data is being transmitted across networks, such as
when you access a website using a browser
Encryption at rest: This is when data is being stored on a storage medium, such as a

86727.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
86727.heading: Chapter 17 478
86727.content:
hard drive
AWS offers services to help you design and implement encryption for data both in transit and
at rest.
For data in transit, you must idx_f20d6e55 transmit the data using Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer
Security (SSL/TLS). This idx_dca472cd requires the sending and receiving nodes to establish a secure
connection, such as the HTTPS protocol. To establish the encrypted connection, you must use
X.509 certificates that you can either purchase from a third-party certificate authority or idx_7913925f create
using the AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) service.
To protect data at rest, you must create an encryption key to encrypt and decrypt data as it is
stored and retrieved from a given storage medium, such as an Amazon EBS volume or an EFS
file store. Encryption and decryption keys are data files containing a long series of numbers
and/or letters that are used by a cryptographic algorithm to encode and decode data. Examples
of algorithms you idx_d5debcfa may idx_eeb08fad have heard idx_392c5fff of include Triple DES or Advanced Encryption Standard
(AES-256) encryption.
An encryption key can be either symmetric or asymmetric:
Symmetric keys use the same key idx_bd8362fe for both encrypting and decrypting the data.
Asymmetric keys are a combination idx_ce04b15f of a public/private key pair. You use the public
key to encrypt the data, and only someone who has access to the private key of that
pair can decrypt it.
In an on-premises environment, you may need to procure the necessary infrastructure to create
and manage encryption and decryption keys, as well as perform the actual task of encrypting

and decrypting data idx_b498ea10 yourself. However, AWS offers its Key Management Service (KMS),
which takes away much of the underlying heavy lifting from you.
With KMS, you can create and idx_e1d4e554 manage customer-managed keys (CMKs), which are used in
conjunction with AWS services that integrate with KMS to encrypt the data those services store
on your behalf. Using customer-managed keys gives you a higher level of control over the
lifecycle and usage of your keys.
AWS also provides AWS-managed keys, which are created and managed automatically by
AWS on behalf of a idx_24eb4c09 service (for example, aws/ebs or aws/rds). These keys are free to use but
offer limited control compared to customer-managed keys and are commonly used as the
default encryption option for many AWS services.
You can also use AWS-owned keys if you do not want the overhead of managing keys or
paying for customer-managed idx_98ba90e8 keys. AWS-owned keys are fully managed by AWS and are used
automatically by some services behind the scenes. You can use these keys to encrypt and
decrypt your data, but you do not have control over the lifecycle of the key, and you do not see
them in your account. You are also not charged for using these keys.
The AWS Key Management Service (KMS) uses shared idx_9ece96c4 hardware security modules to
generate the necessary key material that is then used to create your encryption keys. Although
this is highly secure and uses Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS 140-2)
validated idx_5d23103e hardware, it is nevertheless shared with other customers, which means you do not
have complete control over the hardware security modules. In some cases, this might be
unacceptable idx_ce4a8953 depending idx_32ea1f6b on the industry your business operates in.
In the next section, you will learn more about how you can use your own hardware security
modules in the cloud to create and manage your keys.
AWS CloudHSM
AWS CloudHSM is a dedicated idx_c32aacb3 hardware security module (HSM) that allows you to generate
and manage your encryption keys for use with AWS services to encrypt and decrypt your data.
These hardware modules are placed in your VPC and managed by AWS. While AWS takes care
of provisioning these hardware modules, you are fully responsible for generating, storing,
importing, and exporting your cryptographic keys. AWS does not have access to your keys and
cannot recover them if you lose those keys. It is recommended that you have at least a
minimum of two CloudHSM devices for failover and to avoid a single point of failure. This
obviously increases the cost, but it is highly advised.
AWS CloudHSM complies with FIPS 140-3 (Level 3) and is ideal when AWS KMS is not enough
from a control, compliance, and trust perspective. For example, a government organization

Protecting your data using encryption technologies is fundamental to enforcing your security
posture. However, you must also ensure that your applications are secured and protected from
malicious idx_889789b1 attacks. In the next section, you will learn about an AWS service designed to protect
your application from common web exploits and attacks.
Protecting web applications with AWS WAF
AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF) is designed to offer firewall protection at the
application layer, protecting idx_f7497a7e your idx_846e04cf workloads over standard HTTP and HTTPS protocols. The
service integrates with various application layer entry points published through Amazon
CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, and Application Load Balancers.
This allows you to protect your applications against common web exploits such as cross-site
scripting and SQL injection attacks. With AWS WAF, you create web access control lists (web
ACLs), define rules that fall within specific criteria, and specify the actions to take if any web
request matches that criterion, such as dropping requests suspected to be malicious.
Next, you will learn about another security tool that helps prevent network attacks.
Mitigating DDoS attacks with AWS Shield
AWS Shield offers idx_3a7c468c protection idx_fa6bac8b against Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks. This is an
attack type where bad actors attempt to overwhelm your applications, networks, and resources
by sending a flood of internet traffic. Your resources cannot cope with the load and end up
denying access to authorized users, resulting in customer dissatisfaction, reputational damage,
and ultimately financial loss.
AWS offers two tiers for the AWS Shield service. These are:
AWS Shield Standard: This is offered idx_08515ead free of cost for AWS customers and protects
against common network and transport layer DDoS attacks on your websites and
applications. AWS Shield Standard can be used with Amazon CloudFront and Route 53
to provide layered protection against known infrastructure attacks. This means that to
benefit from the standard offering, your architecture must make use of these services.
AWS Shield Advanced: This tier offers additional protection against attacks on your
EC2 instances, load balancers, CloudFront distributions, Global Accelerator, and more.
The service offers real-time detection, proactive monitoring, and automatic mitigation
of application layer (Layer 7) attacks. In addition, when you subscribe to the advanced
version, you get access to the AWS Shield Response Team (SRT), an expert idx_fbd53e2a team
available 24/7 for manual intervention and support. AWS also reimburses costs for
scaling resources, such as auto-scaling your EC2 instances due to DDoS attacks.

Identifying vulnerabilities with Amazon Inspector
AWS offers a wide idx_37d0b021 range of tools to protect your network, infrastructure resources as well as
your applications from malicious attacks. However, prevention is always better than cure, and
one such service that you must add to your toolkit is AWS Inspector. This service continuously
assesses the network exposure and software vulnerabilities of your EC2, Lambda functions,
and code scans, as well as container workloads.
With AWS Inspector, you can detect open ports and identify whether the operating system or
applications running on your instances are known to have vulnerabilities that need to be
patched.
AWS Inspector integrates with AWS Systems Manager to collect telemetry data from your
instances. The service automatically scans your workloads and compares findings against
security intelligence idx_fd1a6736 sources such as the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE)
database.
AWS Inspector evaluates:
Network exposure: Identifying instances that may be reachable from the internet
Software vulnerabilities: Detecting known vulnerabilities in operating systems and
installed applications
The findings are idx_f9b54907 presented in the AWS Inspector dashboard with granular data to help you
identify potential vulnerabilities. You can then take necessary action to resolve these.
While analyzing your EC2 instances, Lambda code, and containers to detect vulnerabilities is
crucial, you must also ensure that your data is protected from unauthorized access.
Specifically, you must ensure that idx_09ca2563 you protect personally identifiable information (PII) and
track how it is being used, enforcing guardrails to prevent unauthorized access.
This is where services such as Amazon Macie, GuardDuty, and Detective become useful, as they
help you identify sensitive data, detect suspicious activity, and investigate potential security
issues across your AWS environment.

Amazon Macie
Amazon Macie is a fully managed idx_a1c59651 data security and privacy service designed to help protect
Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and Protected Health Information (PHI) stored idx_88842503
in your idx_5adc89f9 Amazon S3 buckets.
Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern-matching capabilities to discover sensitive
data and track changes to your buckets by identifying new or modified objects over time. The
service can be used to perform on-demand analysis or run automated data discovery jobs,
reporting its findings through dashboards and alerts.
Amazon Macie can also be used in a multi-account architecture by monitoring your buckets
across multiple accounts within an AWS Organizations configuration. This means you can
designate a single Macie administrator account to centrally manage and help prevent data
leaks across all member accounts.
In the next section, you will learn about another service designed to detect malicious activity
against your AWS account.
AWS GuardDuty
AWS GuardDuty is idx_ec0c9508 a threat detection service designed to help you identify potential malicious
activity against your AWS accounts and applications.
The service uses various threat intelligence feeds, such as known malicious IP addresses and
domains, and applies machine learning to analyze data from Amazon CloudTrail event logs,
VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 DNS logs.
AWS GuardDuty can detect the use of compromised credentials, communication with
malicious IP addresses, as well as unusual activity carried out in your AWS account based on
past behavior — for example, if a fleet of EC2 instances is launched in a region you do not
normally operate in, or if Amazon S3 API calls originate from an unexpected remote host, or if
unauthorized access attempts are made from known malicious IP addresses.

Amazon Detective

accessible only to authorized entities.
AWS aligns with industry best practices, compliance programs, and regulatory requirements,

Nevertheless, how you design your application is just as important in ensuring that your

Cloud Economics and
AWS Pricing
One major reason for moving to the cloud is the promise of moving from a CapEx mode of
investment in IT to an OpEx mode – meaning that as an organization, you are charged for your
IT services on a pay-as-you-go model or, more importantly, on a pay-as-you-consume model.
This is analogous to how you pay for electricity, gas, or water supply. Ultimately, this means
that you do not have to tie up vast amounts of capital in hardware infrastructure that you must
procure if you were self-hosting resources to host your applications. However, cloud can
become very expensive really quickly if you do not plan your solutions well, if you leave unused
resources running, and if you are not diligent to avoid waste.
This penultimate part focuses on cloud economics and the AWS billing and pricing models,
enabling you to design your solutions in the most cost-effective manner. You must learn the
fundamentals of how AWS charges for its services, where you can save on costs through
volume pricing or reserving capacity, and how to calculate your estimated monthly costs using
the tools provided. FinOps is a huge career pathway you can consider, and this part of the AWS
Certified Cloud Practitioner study guide introduces the core concepts of cost optimization in
the cloud.
This part of the book includes only the following chapter:

86753.heading: Chapter 18, Cloud Economics and Pricing Strategies on AWS •
86753.content:
Chapter 18, Cloud Economics and Pricing Strategies on AWS •
18
Cloud Economics and Pricing
Strategies on AWS
Companies often consider moving to the cloud because they have heard about the cost benefits
associated with shifting from a CAPEX model of IT investment to an OPEX model. CAPEX
refers to capital expenditure associated with procuring hardware such as servers, storage, and
networking equipment. Although these can be considered assets for the business, it is worth
bearing in mind that such assets often depreciate very quickly and inevitably need to be
replaced. Computing hardware typically has a lifecycle of around three to five years, and that
does not even consider the replacement of failed hardware components during that time.
OPEX, on the other hand, refers to operational expenses, which can vary depending on usage
and consumption. Unlike CAPEX, where once you purchase hardware, the cost remains the
same regardless of whether you fully utilize it or not, OPEX allows you to benefit from a pay-
as-you-consume model. This helps organizations operate more cost-efficiently because they
only pay for the resources they use. Depending on how you design and build your solutions
and architectures, the overall IT spend can be significantly lower compared to following a
traditional CAPEX model.
Cloud providers invest massive amounts of capital into computing infrastructure and make
those resources available to customers through this pay-as-you-go consumption model. This
ultimately gives organizations the opportunity to reduce their overall IT expenses while
maintaining flexibility and scalability.
In this chapter, you will learn about some basic cost optimization principles, followed by a
review of some specific tools and services to help you manage your costs more effectively.
The following are the main topics covered in this chapter:
Learning the fundamentals of AWS billing and pricing strategies •
Introducing AWS cost calculators (Pricing Calculator)
Estimating migration costs with Migration Evaluator
Understanding the basics of AWS Cost Explorer
Configuring AWS Budgets
Learning the fundamentals of AWS billing and
pricing strategies
As a minimum, AWS charges idx_716d721a you for the resources you consume based on three primary core
elements:
Amount of computing capacity: For instance, the EC2 or RDS instance type you use
for a given number of seconds
Storage: The total storage consumed; for example, 100 GB of EBS GP3 Volume
Outbound data transfer: The total data transferred out of a region, for example, 1 TB
of data transfer from eu-west-2 (London region) to your local data center
The following subsections provide a broad overview of how you might strategically choose the
resource types idx_30e5fc65 you use to optimize costs.
Compute services
How you are idx_af5a4a02 charged for your compute resources idx_c1851e0c depends very much on the pricing model you

86754.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
86754.heading: Chapter 18, Cloud Economics and Pricing Strategies on AWS •
86754.content:
choose. For example, if you deploy an EC2 instance idx_dfc436d1 using the On-Demand pricing model, you
pay a fixed rate per second (with a 60-second minimum) depending on the instance type that
defines the CPU, memory, storage, and network capabilities.
You could also idx_aca3d2b1 purchase a Reserved Instance for the same instance and benefit from a
discounted hourly rate. The level of discount varies depending on the length of the reservation,
such as a 1-year or 3-year term, and whether you choose to pay for the reservation all upfront,
partially upfront, or with a no-upfront payment option.
The decision to choose between On-Demand and Reserved Instances depends on your use
case. If you plan to have your instances running 24/7 throughout the year, then you will benefit
from purchasing those instances using the Reserved Instance pricing model. Bear in mind that
regardless of your consumption patterns, once you purchase a Reserved Instance, you are

Storage services
Depending on the type idx_9ee757ee of storage you consume, you are charged based on the total storage
allocated or consumed, plus additional parameters, such as the number of requests made to
your storage service. Pricing will also vary depending on the region your storage resource is
created in. The following provides a broad-level overview of this:
Amazon S3: You are charged for the total storage costs of your object's size and how
long you store the objects for each month. The cost also depends on the storage class
you place your objects in. Additional features such as monitoring and automated
transitions between classes are also applicable for S3 Intelligent-Tiering, as are per-
request ingest charges when using PUT, COPY, or lifecycle rules to move data between
storage classes.
Amazon EBS Volumes: You are charged for the total volume you provision, regardless
of whether you consume that storage or not. Additional charges may be incurred
depending on the volume type and the number of provisioned IOPS (Input/Output
Operations Per Second). You are also charged for snapshots you create, store, and copy
across regions. You will find more details at https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/.
EFS File Systems: With EFS file systems, you pay for the storage you consume.
However, there are also charges based on the type of storage, such as Standard,
Infrequent Access, or Archive, as well as the throughput configuration.

You can tag most idx_3dd5b943 resources you create in AWS to help you identify that resource and what

You can also use cost-allocation tags to help you identify your spending patterns against your
resources. Here, AWS offers two types of cost-allocation tagging options:

User-defined tags: These are created and managed by you using your preferred
corporate naming conventions. These tags help you track usage and cost across your

Businesses move to the cloud to become more agile, access cutting-edge technologies to gain a

AWS provides two key frameworks designed to help organizations successfully navigate their

The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) – which outlines how organizations
plan and manage their cloud transformation initiatives
The AWS Well-Architected Framework (WAF) – which provides best practices for

Understanding the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework
The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) provides a structured approach to help
organizations plan and idx_852969d1 execute their cloud transformation through four key transformation
domains—Technology, Process, Organization, and Product. The following is a high-level
overview of these domains:
Technology: Focuses on cloud services to help migrate and modernize legacy systems,
ultimately reducing costs, improving security posture, and decreasing downtime
Process: Focuses on digitizing, automating, and optimizing business operations. This
may involve using cutting-edge technologies like machine learning and artificial
intelligence to improve customer experience, enhance employee productivity, conduct
fraud detection, and accurately forecast business performance
Organization: Focuses on enhancing teams and departments to better collaborate and
work efficiently together, enabling rapid iterative improvements to products and
services while gaining a competitive advantage
Product: Focuses on creating value propositions and new revenue streams, enabling
organizations to reach more customers and increase market share
These domains represent the primary areas of change required to enable successful cloud
adoption.

Security, and Operations—which together enable organizations to achieve key business
